generic: Sodium Feredetate (Sodium Ironedetate, Sodium Iron EDTA)
quick: Provides ~ elemental iron 100-200 mg/day (commonly sodium feredetate 231 mg = 27.5 mg iron per 5 mL; multiple spoonfuls daily)
Best on an empty stomach; take with food if GI upset occurs
Used to treat/prevent iron deficiency in pregnancy
Use with caution; no specific adjustment usually needed
Caution in significant liver disease / iron overload states
Excess alcohol may increase iron absorption - moderate
Hemoglobin, ferritin, serum iron; response to therapy
summary: Sodium feredetate (sodium iron EDTA) is a well-tolerated oral iron preparation, most often used as a pediatric and adult syrup to treat and prevent iron-deficiency anemia. The iron is held in a stable EDTA chelate that is reasonably bioavailable and tends to cause fewer gastrointestinal complaints than conventional ferrous salts. It is dosed by elemental iron content. As with all iron supplements, accidental overdose is particularly dangerous in young children. (Regional/BNF-type product, not a US FDA-approved iron monograph.)
indications: Treatment of iron-deficiency anemia in adults and children
Prophylaxis of iron deficiency in at-risk groups (infants, children, pregnancy, poor dietary intake)

dosage.d: Elemental iron ~100-200 mg/day in divided doses (e.g., sodium feredetate syrup 27.5 mg iron/5 mL, several 5 mL doses daily)
dosage.n: Continue 3 months after hemoglobin normalizes to replenish stores

dosage.d: Elemental iron ~3-6 mg/kg/day in 1-3 divided doses (using the iron content of the syrup)
dosage.n: Adjust to age/weight; use the elemental-iron figure

dosage.d: Lower elemental iron dose (e.g., ~30-60 mg/day) once daily

admin: Doses are expressed as elemental iron - check the iron content of the specific syrup/tablet
Take preferably on an empty stomach (between meals) for best absorption; if it upsets the stomach, take with food
Use the supplied measuring device for syrups; for liquid drops avoid contact with teeth or dilute and rinse to limit staining
Separate from tea, coffee, dairy, antacids, and certain drugs by ~2 hours
moa: Sodium feredetate delivers iron as a stable ferric-EDTA chelate. After absorption, iron is incorporated into hemoglobin, myoglobin, and iron-dependent enzymes, correcting iron-deficiency anemia. The EDTA chelate keeps iron soluble and protects it from dietary inhibitors, giving relatively consistent bioavailability with comparatively good gastrointestinal tolerability.

absolute: Anemias not due to iron deficiency (e.g., hemolytic anemia unless iron-deficient)
relative: Active peptic ulcer, ulcerative colitis, or regional enteritis
Children (overdose risk - keep out of reach)
monitor: Symptoms of iron overload with long-term use

preg: Iron-deficiency anemia is common and treatable in pregnancy. Sodium feredetate is used to treat and prevent iron deficiency during pregnancy; use as indicated with monitoring of hemoglobin and ferritin.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding. Iron requirements are increased postpartum, and oral iron supplementation is appropriate when indicated.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment, but no specific dose adjustment is generally required for oral iron. In dialysis/erythropoietin-treated patients, iron status should be assessed (parenteral iron may be preferred).
hepatic: Use with caution in significant hepatic impairment and avoid in iron-overload-associated liver disease, as excess iron can accumulate and worsen hepatic injury.

moderate: Oral tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones (mutual reduced absorption - separate doses)
Levothyroxine, levodopa, methyldopa, bisphosphonates, penicillamine (reduced absorption - separate by 2-4 h)
Antacids, calcium, magnesium, proton pump inhibitors (reduced iron absorption)
minor: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) enhances iron absorption
Tea, coffee, dairy, eggs, bran (reduce iron absorption)
interactions.food: Best on empty stomach; food, tea, dairy reduce absorption; vitamin C increases it
interactions.alcohol: Excessive alcohol may increase iron absorption and stores
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause false-positive occult blood tests; alters serum iron and ferritin values

serious: Iron overload with chronic excessive use
GI mucosal irritation/ulceration with prolonged contact
emergency: Acute iron poisoning (especially in children) - vomiting, hematemesis, shock

monitoring: Hemoglobin and reticulocyte count to confirm response
Serum ferritin and iron studies to guide duration and detect overload
counsel: Take preferably between meals; if it upsets your stomach, take with food
Stools may turn black - this is normal and harmless
Keep well out of the reach of children - iron overdose can be fatal in small children
Separate from tea, coffee, milk, antacids, and certain medicines by a couple of hours
Continue for the full course to rebuild iron stores, even after blood counts improve
pk: Reticulocyte response in ~5-10 days; hemoglobin rises over weeks
Iron absorption occurs mainly in the duodenum/upper jejunum after dosing
Body iron is largely recycled and conserved; not characterized by a simple plasma half-life
Continue 2-3 months after hemoglobin normalizes to replenish stores
Store below 25-30 C; keep syrup tightly closed; protect from light; keep out of children's reach
pearls: Dose by elemental iron, not by salt weight - check the product's iron content
Iron-EDTA chelate is generally better tolerated and less affected by dietary inhibitors than ferrous sulfate
Vitamin C enhances absorption; tea, dairy, antacids, and PPIs reduce it
Accidental iron ingestion is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in young children - storage counseling is essential (regional/BNF product, not a single US FDA monograph)
missed: Take the missed dose when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next dose, then skip it. Do not double up. Occasional missed doses do not materially affect a course of iron therapy.
overdose: Iron overdose is a medical emergency, particularly in children. Early features: vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, hematemesis; later: shock, metabolic acidosis, hepatic failure. Management includes assessing serum iron, whole-bowel irrigation for large ingestions, and IV deferoxamine chelation for severe poisoning. Seek emergency/poison-center care.
